notes_list.title: Gerund (-ing) vs Infinitive (to + verb)
notes_list.basic_overview: Gerund: real, completed or past experience (I enjoy reading). Infinitive: goal, potential or future (I plan to read).
notes_list.extra_info_content: Tests: after a preposition (of, for, about, at, in, by) always a gerund (tired of working). After an adjective (difficult, happy, important) use an infinitive (difficult to learn). Subject of a sentence = gerund (Swimming is great exercise); purpose = infinitive (I am here to study).

notes_list.title: Meaning Changes with Gerund / Infinitive
notes_list.basic_overview: Remember locking = recall that you already locked the door. Remember to lock = a future reminder.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Stop smoking = quit the habit. Stop to smoke = pause another activity in order to smoke.

notes_list.title: Uncountable Nouns Used Only in Singular
notes_list.basic_overview: Words like furniture, scenery, machinery, stationery, poetry, jewellery, crockery, luggage, baggage, breakage, percentage, knowledge, information, traffic, coffee, dust are always singular.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 'Furnitures' is wrong; the plural of furniture is furniture. Correct: All the furniture was burnt down by the fire. Uncountable nouns need a unit word (2 kg sugar, 1 glass water).

notes_list.title: One of the + Plural Noun
notes_list.basic_overview: The noun after 'one of the' is always plural: One of the + plural noun + that/who + verb.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Correct: One of the reasons behind malnutrition is the improper way of food intake.

notes_list.title: Relative Pronoun 'that'
notes_list.basic_overview: After qualifiers like the same, only, all, nothing, everything and superlatives, use 'that' as the relative pronoun.
notes_list.extra_info_content: This is the same man that met me in the market yesterday ('who', 'whom' and 'which' are not suitable here).

notes_list.title: Possessive Apostrophe
notes_list.basic_overview: Singular noun: add 's (Rahul's car, the dog's bone). Plural noun already ending in s: add only the apostrophe (students' books).
notes_list.extra_info_content: Irregular plurals not ending in s take 's (children's toys).

notes_list.title: Question Tags
notes_list.basic_overview: A short question is added to a statement: positive statement takes a negative tag and vice versa (It's hot today, isn't it?).
notes_list.extra_info_content: For 'I am', the standard tag is 'aren't I?' ('am not I' is non-standard). Example: I am late for the meeting, aren't I?

notes_list.title: Inversion after 'Not only'
notes_list.basic_overview: When 'Not only' begins the sentence, the first clause uses question word order (inversion).
notes_list.extra_info_content: Correct: Not only is he a great athlete, but he is also a brilliant student.

notes_list.title: 'Yet' with Although / Despite
notes_list.basic_overview: Do not use 'yet' in the second part with although, despite or in spite of; it is superfluous.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 'Despite' is a preposition; 'yet' is a conjunction meaning but/nevertheless. 'Yet' can also be an adverb meaning 'up to now'.

notes_list.title: When / Then / Than; More / Most
notes_list.basic_overview: When = time (kab). Then = next in sequence (First study, then play). Than = comparison (Tea is better than coffee).
notes_list.extra_info_content: More = comparative (two things): more interesting than that one. Most = superlative (three or more): the most interesting book in the library.

notes_list.title: Indirect Speech with 'need'
notes_list.basic_overview: Modal 'need' (need not) stays unchanged in indirect speech with a reporting verb like told: Sita told her friend that she need not study so hard.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Main verb 'need' (meaning require) changes: She said, 'I need money' becomes She said that she needed money. For an interrogative sentence use asked/enquired, not told: He asked me if he had to stay there.
